h1: The 6 Best Food Processors Under $100 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Food Processors Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 6 best food processors under $100, from 3-cup minis to 10-cup meal-prep bowls, compared on capacity and functions.
summary: The Cuisinart 4-Cup with an auto-reversing SmartPower blade is the best overall: a real processor in a compact body for under $50. The Hamilton Beach 10-Cup is the meal prep pick, the 8-Cup is the mid-size family option, and the Cuisinart FP-5 adds shredding. The Hamilton Beach 3-Cup and Cuisinart Mini are choppers for small batches.
intro: The usual food processor mistake is buying the biggest bowl the budget allows. Below $100, capacity and capability pull in opposite directions. A 10-cup bowl slices and shreds a week of vegetables, but a 3-cup mini does a single onion or a batch of dip better than a half-empty giant, because the blade has food to catch instead of spinning in air.

Our editors reviewed six models from their listings, comparing bowl size, blade design and the functions each states. Choppers that did not list a clear blade design lost points. The ranking favors machines that match a real kitchen routine, whether that means weekly meal prep or a spoonful of pesto, over those that simply offer the largest number on the box.

products.name: Cuisinart Small Food Processor, Auto-Reversing Smart Power Blade, 4-Cup
products.verdict: A real processor in a compact size, under $50.
products.description:
The 4-cup Cuisinart earns its place with the SmartPower blade, which reverses direction. It cuts on one side, then flips to the blunt side to push food back toward the blades, so chunks do not stay stuck at the top of the bowl. A compact base and a price in the $25 to $50 bucket make it easy to keep on the counter.

It leads because a reversing blade is a processor feature that a plain chopper lacks. The Hamilton Beach models offer more bowl, but they cost a larger footprint, and the FP-5 costs more without adding reversing.

Buy it for a small household that wants a true processor for salsa, hummus and slaw. The caveat: a 4-cup bowl limits batch size, so a family meal prep session takes several rounds.
products.idealFor: Small households that want a true processor.
products.skipIf: You prep big batches for the week.

products.name: Hamilton Beach Food Processor & Vegetable Chopper, 10 Cups, Stainless Steel
products.verdict: The most bowl space under $100, with an Easy Clean scraper.
products.description:
The 10-cup Hamilton Beach is the most bowl you can buy in this price range, with slicing, shredding, mincing and puree functions and a stainless steel blade. A built-in Easy Clean scraper clears the sides of the bowl, which saves stopping to scrape by hand in the middle of a batch.

It ranks second to the Cuisinart on convenience, not capability. Against it you gain 6 cups of volume and more functions, at the cost of counter space. It also beats the 8-cup sibling by two cups and the scraper, which the smaller model does not list.

Choose it for meal prep, big salads and larger households. The caveat is storage: a 10-cup base is awkward in a small kitchen, and it is overkill for one person who mostly chops a single onion.
products.skipIf: Your kitchen is small or you cook for one.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 8 Cup Food Processor & Vegetable Chopper
products.verdict: Eight cups and a vegetable chopper mode for a moderate budget.
products.description:
The 8-cup Hamilton Beach offers slicing, shredding, mincing and pureeing, plus a vegetable chopper mode, for $50 to $100. That mix covers most family cooking: sliced cucumbers for dinner, grated cheese for tacos, smooth soup base at the end.

It ranks third because its 10-cup sibling adds two cups of capacity and an Easy Clean scraper, which this model does not list. The 8-cup suits those who want the same function list in a slightly smaller body, and the lower cost reflects that.

Pick it for a family kitchen that does not batch cook weekly. Skip it if you only chop small amounts, because a big bowl underperforms on a single onion. The missing scraper means more stopping to push food down by hand.

products.name: Cuisinart 5-Cup Chop & Shred Food Processor FP-5
products.verdict: A 5-cup chop and shred machine that stores easily.
products.description:
The FP-5 is a 5-cup Cuisinart built for chopping and shredding, with an easy-store compact design. It sits between the mini choppers and the full-size Hamilton Beach models, and it is the one machine here that gives you a shredding disc in a small body.

It ranks fourth because it costs more than the 4-cup Cuisinart without adding a reversing blade, and the listing does not mention slicing or pureeing. The shredding is the reason to buy it instead.

Buy it if you grate cheese and vegetables often and want a Cuisinart in a body that fits a cabinet. Skip it if you want slicing or puree functions, since the listing names neither. At $50 to $100, the Hamilton Beach 8-cup offers more functions for a similar outlay.
products.idealFor: Cooks who want basic shredding in a compact unit.
products.skipIf: You want slicing and pureeing too.

products.name: Hamilton Beach 3 Cup Electric Vegetable Chopper & Mini Food Processor
products.description:
The 3-cup Hamilton Beach is the lowest-priced option in the guide, under $25. A single-touch operation means you press the top and the blade runs, with no mode dial to confuse anyone. The compact body suits quick jobs like onions, garlic and herbs.

It ranks fifth because it lacks the Cuisinart mini's reversible stainless blade and has only a basic function set. It wins on price and simplicity.

Buy it for fast chopping and nothing more. The caveat is size: three cups is a small bowl, so a cup of chopped onion and a few carrots can fill it. It cannot slice or shred. Treat it as a faster knife for prep, and you will be satisfied.
products.idealFor: Quick chopping of onions and herbs.

products.name: Cuisinart Mini Food Processor, Reversible Blade, 3-Cup Capacity
products.verdict: A reversible stainless blade for small-batch purees.
products.description:
The Cuisinart Mini has a 3-cup bowl, a reversible stainless blade and a compact body, for $25 to $50. It is built for small batches: pesto, hummus, salsa and sauces that need to be smooth, where a blender would be wasteful.

It finishes last because the 4-cup Cuisinart offers a bigger bowl and an auto-reversing blade for similar money. This one is for small batches only, and small batches is a narrow job.

Buy it if you make dips and sauces in small amounts and want Cuisinart build quality. The caveat is clear: it is not for meal prep, and a three cup bowl fills quickly with raw vegetables. For anything beyond a few servings, step up to the 4-cup Cuisinart.

whatMatters.detail: Bowl size is measured in cups of capacity and sets how much you can process at once. A 3-cup bowl handles a single onion, while a 10-cup bowl handles a week of vegetables. Too large and the blade spins in air on small amounts. Check the cup number in the title and match it to your usual batch.

Slicing, shredding, mincing and pureeing are separate tasks that need different blades or discs, and a chopper only minces. Many listings blur this. Look for the function list on the listing before assuming a machine slices or shreds. The Hamilton Beach 8 and 10 cup models list four functions, and the mini choppers list one.

A reversing blade changes direction to cut, then flips to push food back toward the knife edge, which improves results. Plain blades can leave chunks stuck on the side or top of the bowl. Check whether the listing names a reversing or reversible blade, as the Cuisinart 4-cup and Mini do, and what it is made of.

Big bowls need big bases and cabinet space, and a 10-cup unit is awkward in a small kitchen. A processor that lives in a cupboard gets used less. Compare the listed size or category to your storage before buying. Measure the shelf height, because tall bowls and lids rarely fit under standard cabinets.

Features like a bowl scraper reduce the work of getting food out, and fewer parts are easier to wash. The Hamilton Beach 10-cup lists an Easy Clean scraper, which saves stopping to scrape. Look for scraper or dishwasher notes in the bullets, and count how many separate parts you will be washing after every use.

faq.q: Can a mini processor replace a full-size one?
faq.a: For small batches, yes. A 3-cup bowl cannot handle full meal prep, so choose the 8 or 10 cup Hamilton Beach for that. The Cuisinart mini suits dips and sauces well, but it fills quickly with raw vegetables.

faq.q: What mistake do buyers make with food processors?
faq.a: Buying the largest bowl. A big bowl underperforms on small amounts, so match capacity to your typical batch. A 4-cup Cuisinart handles most daily cooking and stores more easily than a 10-cup unit, which matters in a small kitchen.

faq.q: Is the Cuisinart worth it over the Hamilton Beach?
faq.a: For compact kitchens, yes, thanks to the reversing blade and small footprint. For meal prep, the Hamilton Beach 10-cup offers more space and functions, though it takes more room and costs more to store.

faq.q: How do I use the pulse function well?
faq.a: Pulse in short bursts rather than running continuously, which gives even chunks instead of mush. Stop and check the texture often, especially with the 3-cup choppers, where food moves quickly and over-processing happens in a second or two.

faq.q: How do I clean a food processor?
faq.a: Rinse the parts right after use so food does not dry on, and check the listing for dishwasher notes. Be careful with the blades, which are sharp and should be washed by hand with a brush.

Listings here do not state it, so let food cool before processing, and check the manual. Hot liquid can build pressure in a closed bowl, which is why caution is wise. Work in small batches if you must handle warm food.

finalTake: Buy the Cuisinart 4-Cup for most small households, and the Hamilton Beach 10-Cup if you prep for the week or cook for a crowd. The 8-Cup suits families that want the same functions with a smaller body. Choose the 3-cup models only for onions, herbs, dips and sauces, never for full meals.
